implementation_notes: C++20 replaces the classic hand-rolled arrangement (an atomic cancel flag plus a condition-variable notification) with two stdlib pieces: std::chrono::steady_clock::time_point as the monotonic deadline value and std::stop_token/stop_source as the cooperative cancellation handle. The coupling point is the interruptible wait - condition_variable_any::wait_until(lock, stoken, abs_time, pred) registers for the stop request and the deadline at once, so a cancelled or expired request wakes even without a notification. Forward the same time_point plus a stop_token across call boundaries (bridge the parent signal with a stop_callback into a child stop_source) and never compute a fresh full timeout per hop. Sibling variant: when the hop's transport is already gRPC, prefer the runtime-provided deadline propagation on ClientContext instead of hand-wiring the tokens.
pitfalls: std::stop_token only interrupts waits that accept it (condition_variable_any::wait_until, jthread, the std::execution library); a plain std::future::get() or blocking socket read ignores it and still needs the remaining time as its own timeout.

The wait_until overload converts abs_time internally and implementations fall back to system-clock-based pthread_cond_timedwait, so a system clock adjustment can produce a spurious timeout even when steady_clock was passed.
A stop_source must outlive the tokens taken from it; keeping only a stop_token in a long-lived continuation after the source dies leaves a token that can never be stopped.
Requesting stop on the parent does not stop child sources automatically: create a child stop_source per hop and bridge it with std::stop_callback, or cancellation dies at the boundary.

variants.name: gRPC C++ deadline propagation via ClientContext::FromServerContext
variants.implementation_notes: When the hop's transport is gRPC, its runtime already carries deadlines: the client sets one on grpc::ClientContext (set_deadline), the server receives the incoming call's budget, and grpc::ClientContext::FromServerContext(server_ctx, PropagationOptions) forks a client context from the incoming server call so its deadline and cancellation follow - the gRPC deadlines guide notes that C++ requires this explicit enablement where Java and Go propagate by default. Use set_deadline for hand-rolled call sites and TryCancel() to signal a local give-up back into the call. Bounds and the remaining-time conversion stay inside the runtime, which is why this variant wins whenever the stack is already gRPC.
pitfalls: C++ does not enable automatic propagation by default (the gRPC guide names C++ explicitly): without FromServerContext() or set_deadline each outgoing call starts with no deadline and the chain degrades into fresh timeouts.
A ClientContext must not be reused across RPCs and must stay alive and valid for the lifetime of the call; storing or sharing a FromServerContext result beyond the handler is a lifetime bug.
Server-side cancellation is only visible to code that checks it or passes it down: the runtime aborts the call, not the application's work.
Hand-written interceptors must subtract elapsed time before setting a deadline on the outgoing call rather than copying the incoming instant blindly.
